Problem statement

Finding blood still runs on phone calls and forwards

Patients’ families

An urgent need turns into phone calls and forwarded posts. Nobody can tell who has seen the request or who is on the way.

Willing donors

They do not know which centre needs their blood group, whether they are eligible today, or when a slot is free.

Blood centres

Stock levels are hidden from donors, and donors rarely hear what happened to their blood — so fewer come back.

Our problem statement: design a mobile app that lets a willing donor find a centre, check eligibility and book a slot in a few taps, and lets a patient’s family send an urgent request to nearby compatible donors — then follow every step live.

Scope of this CA-3

Users

Who we designed for: three proto-personas

Aarav Deshpande · Donor

Primary user · B+ · Kothrud, Pune · 6 donations since 2021

  • Wants to know when he can donate again and book without paperwork.
  • Wants to see where his blood went.
  • Frustrated by forms at every centre and no news after donating.

Meera’s family · Requester

Primary user · needs 2 units of B+ at Sahyadri Hospital within 6 hours

  • Wants to reach compatible donors fast, without knowing transfusion rules.
  • Wants to know who is coming and when.
  • Frustrated by panic, guesswork and no status updates.

Blood-centre staff

Secondary user · blood bank desk at a hospital

  • Wants donors who arrive eligible and on time.
  • Wants quick check-in and verified donor details.
  • Frustrated by deferrals at the desk and repeated paperwork.

Proto-personas are assumption-based (Cooper, 1999). They guided our design decisions and should be validated with real donors and families in usability testing.

Fast under stress

An urgent request fits on one screen; big primary buttons sit at the bottom, in thumb reach.

Trustworthy

Verified donors, government-licensed centres and stock that says when it was last updated.

Private by default

A hospital sees a donor’s number only after the donor accepts the request.

Clear

One question per screen, plain words, and “Why do we ask this?” next to medical questions.

Motivating

A “ready to donate” countdown, an impact tracker and badges bring donors back.

Accessible

Large touch targets, colour never used alone, visible focus states.

Warm neutrals keep the app calm; red is kept for actions and urgency. The same token names are used as Figma variables and as CSS custom properties.

Design system · Figma

Reusable components and one icon family

  • Button — primary, secondary and outline, in 56 px and 44 px heights.
  • Blood-group chip — default and selected; works as a radio button.
  • Filter chip — off and on; works as a checkbox.
  • Status tag — critical, ready, soon, neutral: a dot, a colour and a word.
  • Input field — default, focused and error with helper text.
  • Android system bars, top app bar, bottom navigation (four active states).
Icons · Phosphor, Regular + Fill

One stroke style everywhere; the filled version marks the active tab and selected states.

Flow 01 · Onboarding

Sign up in three short steps

  • Welcome — one clear promise, one main button; “Skip” and “Sign in” for returning donors.
  • Sign in — only a mobile number; explains up front that hospitals see it only after you accept.
  • OTP — large keypad, resend timer, and “Change” if the number was wrong.
  • Blood group — tap one of 8 chips instead of typing; “I don’t know” is a valid answer.
HCI principles applied
Visibility of status: Step 1 of 3User controlRecognition over recallError recovery
Flow 02 · Home & discover

Know when you can donate, and where

  • Home — a status card says “You’re ready to donate again”; urgent requests show only patients the donor’s group can help.
  • Find — map plus list; filter chips such as “Has B+” and “Within 5 km”.
  • Centre — stock for all 8 groups with a text legend and “Updated 10 min ago”.
  • Eligibility — one question per screen, progress shown, and a “Why do we ask this?” note.
HCI principles applied
Match with the real worldHick’s lawHelp in contextError prevention
Flow 03 · Book a donation

Booking a slot, then closure

  • Donation type — a two-option segmented control shows how long each one takes (45 min vs 2 hrs).
  • Day and time — a date strip and slot grid grouped into Morning / Afternoon; full slots are struck through and cannot be picked.
  • Sticky summary — the chosen slot and the Confirm button stay at the bottom, within thumb reach.
  • Confirmation — token number, QR code for fast check-in, a “Before you come” checklist, Add to calendar and Directions.
HCI principles applied
Gestalt proximityFitts’s lawClosure (Shneiderman)Reduce memory load
Flow 04 · Emergency request

From request to donor arrival, in plain sight

  • Safety first — a banner says to call 108 for an ambulance before anything else.
  • Compatibility done for you — the family picks the patient’s group; the app alerts every compatible group (B+, B−, O+, O−) and says so on the button.
  • Live matching — a darker screen signals urgency: 48 alerted, 31 seen, 6 said yes, nearest first.
  • Tracking — “1 of 2 units arranged”, time left, and a timeline of every update.
HCI principles applied
Visibility of system statusError preventionEmotional designFeedback
Flow 05 · Donor card & impact

Reasons to come back

  • Digital donor card — verified badge, QR code, eligibility, last haemoglobin and blood pressure — no paperwork at the next centre.
  • Impact — “18 people may have been helped by your 6 donations”, with the reason: one unit becomes red cells, plasma and platelets.
  • Where your blood went — Donated → Tested → Sent out → Used, ending with the hospital that used it.
  • Badges and history — small rewards for regular donors, and a record of every donation.
HCI principles applied
Feedback loopHonest wordingRecognitionMotivation
Evaluation · Heuristics

Nielsen’s 10 heuristics, checked against the design

HeuristicWhere Raktdaan applies it
1 Visibility of system status“Step 2 of 3”, “Question 3 of 6 · about a minute left”, live request timeline, stock “updated 10 min ago”
2 Match with the real world+91 numbers, km, Pune hospitals, units in ml, NBTC donor rules, 108 ambulance
3 User control and freedomSkip, Back on every step, “Change” number or centre, pause alerts any time
4 Consistency and standardsOne component library; Android system bars and bottom navigation; main button always at the bottom
5 Error preventionEligibility check before booking; app works out compatible groups; full slots cannot be picked
6 Recognition rather than recallBlood-group chips, date strip and slot grid, QR donor card instead of typing IDs
7 Flexibility and efficiency“I can donate” right on Home; filter chips; Add to calendar; Request is one tap away
8 Aesthetic and minimalist designOne main action per screen; warm, calm palette; red only for actions and urgency
9 Help users recover from errorsInline error text on inputs; “I don’t know my blood group”; OTP resend timer and “Change”
10 Help and documentation“Why do we ask this?”, “Did you know?” tips, “Before you come” checklist

Touch targets and semantics

  • Main buttons are 56 px tall, icon buttons 48 × 48 px, bottom-bar items 76 × 58 px, blood-group chips 76 px tall.
  • Status never relies on colour alone: every tag has a word, and the stock grid has a legend.
  • Choices are real radio buttons and checkboxes (54 inputs); icon-only controls carry text labels (48 aria-labels), so screen readers can announce them.
  • Visible focus ring on every control; animations switch off when “reduce motion” is on.
Result: main text, links and buttons meet WCAG AA contrast, and every touch target is well above the 24 px minimum (WCAG 2.5.8). Ratios are computed from the design tokens in raktdaan.html.
Implementation · HTML & CSS

A clickable prototype with zero JavaScript

  • One file, raktdaan.html: 1,430 lines of HTML and CSS, all 15 screens.
  • Navigation: each screen is a <section id>; buttons are links; CSS :target shows the current screen.
  • State: blood groups, slots, answers and filters are real inputs, styled with :has(:checked).
  • Tokens: CSS custom properties with the same names as the Figma variables; text styles as classes.
  • Icons: 42 Phosphor icons in one inline SVG sprite (<symbol> + <use>).
  • Responsive: on a laptop it shows a phone frame and a screen menu; on a real phone the page becomes the app.
/* 1 · navigation without JavaScript */ .screen { display: none; } .screen:target { display: block; } <a href="#slot" class="btn btn--white">Book a slot</a> /* 2 · selected state from a real radio input */ .bg-chip:has(input:checked) { background: var(--brand); color: var(--text-on-brand); } <label class="bg-chip"> <input class="sr" type="radio" name="my-group" value="B+"> <b>B+</b> … </label>

Conclusion

What we built and what comes next

  • Raktdaan covers both sides of blood donation — a donor’s routine and a family’s emergency — in 15 screens and 5 flows.
  • One design system drives both the Figma file and the HTML & CSS build, so the design and the code match.
  • Our heuristic and WCAG review confirmed clear system status, error prevention, recognition over recall, AA contrast for text and buttons, and large touch targets.
